overview: Haidilao is the world's largest branded hot pot restaurant operator, running 1,389 Haidilao-branded restaurants (as of June 2026) predominantly in mainland China, with a smaller presence in Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan. The company spun off its operations outside Greater China into a separately listed entity, Super Hi International (9658.HK), in late 2022/early 2023, leaving 6862.HK focused on the Chinese Mainland/Greater China hot pot market plus an expanding portfolio of sub-brands and a fast-growing delivery business. Revenue is overwhelmingly generated from self-operated, dine-in restaurants, supplemented by a growing franchise model, condiment/ingredient sales, and a rapidly scaling takeaway ('single-serving fast food') delivery business.

business_model.summary: Haidilao earns the large majority of revenue from self-operated, company-run hot pot restaurants under the core Haidilao brand (table service, dine-in), supplemented by a growing delivery/takeaway business, a nascent and deliberately constrained franchise program, sales of condiments/food ingredients (partly to affiliate Yihai International), and a portfolio of ~20 smaller 'Pomegranate Plan' sub-brands (seafood stalls, sushi, Western light meals, mini hot pot, Chinese fast food). Revenue is largely transactional/per-visit rather than subscription-based, though a >244 million-member loyalty program drives repeat visitation and a 'recurring-like' customer base.

revenue_streams.name: Sales of condiment products and food ingredients

business_model.customer_type: B2C dine-in and delivery consumers across all tiers of Chinese cities, plus Hong Kong/Macau/Taiwan; franchise business is B2B (franchisee operators)
business_model.geographic_mix: Chinese Mainland ~96% of Haidilao restaurant revenue (Tier 1 ~18%, Tier 2 ~37%, Tier 3-and-below ~42%), Hong Kong/Macau/Taiwan ~4%. International operations outside Greater China were spun off into Super Hi International (9658.HK) in Dec 2022/Jan 2023 and are no longer part of 6862.HK.

main_competitors: Yum China's Little Sheep/hot pot concepts
Jiumaojiu's Song Hotpot and other regional hot pot chains
Local/independent hot pot restaurants (highly fragmented market)
Delivery-first and value-oriented casual dining chains
competitive_position.market_position: Largest branded hot pot chain in China by restaurant count and revenue, but operating in a highly fragmented market where branded chains hold a relatively small aggregate share versus thousands of independent hot pot restaurants; market leadership position has weakened as same-store sales and table turnover have declined for several consecutive years amid intensified competition from value-oriented challengers and delivery platforms.

moat_factors.description: Haidilao's name is synonymous with attentive, almost theatrical customer service in China, historically commanding premium pricing and strong word-of-mouth/social media virality.

Scale across 1,300+ self-operated restaurants supports centralized procurement, a shared 'intelligent middle office' for data/ops, and vertically-linked condiment supplier Yihai International (a related party).
Over 244 million registered members as of mid-2026 support precision marketing and repeat visitation, though this has not prevented traffic declines.

Internal/headquarters-driven incubation of sub-brands (food-stall hot pot, sushi, etc.) leverages shared back-office, site-selection and supply-chain capabilities, though this is early-stage and unproven at scale.

Consumers face essentially no switching costs between hot pot restaurants; low barriers to entry in casual dining mean the moat rests almost entirely on brand/service execution rather than structural lock-in.

weaknesses: Heavy reliance on a single core brand (Haidilao dine-in) that is experiencing structural traffic and same-store sales declines
Table turnover rate has fallen from 4.1x/day (2024) to 3.9x/day (2025) and same-store sales fell ~6.7% in 2025, indicating eroding unit economics
Highly fragmented, low-switching-cost industry limits durable pricing power
Execution risk in diversifying into delivery, franchising and sub-brands simultaneously while reorganizing headquarters/middle-office structure
Concentration in Chinese Mainland consumer discretionary spending, which has been soft

growth_drivers: Delivery business ('single-serving high-quality fast food' / rice-bowl takeaway) growing extremely fast (+111.9% in FY2025, +121.2% in H1 2026), now ~9% of revenue and the fastest-growing segment
'Pomegranate Plan' multi-brand incubation (20+ sub-brands, 207 restaurants as of FY2025) shifting from broad exploration to focused replication of proven formats (food-stall hot pot, sushi)
Franchise business expansion (79 franchised Haidilao restaurants at FY2025, up from near zero historically; selectively converting some self-operated stores to franchise to reduce capital intensity)
'Different Haidilao' strategy: themed/scenario restaurants (fresh-cut ingredient concept stores, late-night, family-oriented, pet-friendly) to re-engage price- and experience-sensitive consumers

2026 'middle office' organizational build-out intended to shift growth from single-restaurant-manager-driven execution to centralized, scalable headquarters platform, supporting more disciplined new-store growth in 2027
Potential M&A: management has flagged strategically seeking acquisitions of high-quality catering assets to diversify formats and customer base
Still-low penetration in lower-tier Chinese cities provides a runway for disciplined new restaurant openings

business.risk: Same-store sales and table turnover decline
business.description: Core Haidilao same-store sales fell ~6.7% and table turnover fell from 4.1 to 3.9 times/day in FY2025, continuing a multi-year downtrend driven by competition and changing consumption habits.
Value-oriented hot pot and casual dining challengers, plus third-party delivery platforms, are competing aggressively on price, pressuring both traffic and margins.

Simultaneously scaling delivery, franchising, sub-brands and a new 'middle office' management structure creates meaningful organizational execution risk, as seen in the 2022 restaurant closure cycle ('Woodpecker'/'Hard Bone' plans).
~80-87% of revenue still comes from the core Haidilao dine-in brand, leaving limited diversification despite sub-brand efforts.

financial.description: Core operating profit fell 13.3% in FY2025 despite revenue growth of 1.1%, as raw material costs rose from 37.9% to 40.5% of revenue and delivery-platform/marketing costs increased.
Nearly all revenue and costs are RMB-denominated; dividends are declared in HKD, creating modest translation considerations for HK-listed shareholders.
Significant transactions with affiliated/connected parties (e.g., Yihai International condiment supplier, loans to related entities such as Xi'an Yanqing) require ongoing governance scrutiny.

regulatory.description: As a mass-market restaurant operator, Haidilao is subject to strict and evolving Chinese food safety rules; any publicized food-safety incident could cause significant reputational and revenue damage given its service-reputation-dependent brand.
Cayman Islands holding structure with contractual arrangements (e.g., Shanghai Kiwa) carries typical China-listco structural risk.
Labor costs (~33% of revenue) are sensitive to Chinese minimum wage and social-insurance requirements; staff costs were roughly flat in FY2025 despite revenue growth, reflecting cost discipline.

macro.description: Dine-in casual/mid-tier restaurant spending is discretionary and has been soft amid China's broader consumption slowdown and property-sector-linked wealth effects, directly pressuring Haidilao's core traffic and average spend.
Intense value-for-money competition and food-delivery platform price wars across Chinese catering have compressed industry-wide pricing and margins.
Meat, seafood and vegetable costs (raw materials ~40% of revenue) are exposed to agricultural commodity price swings.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: China's hot pot segment is large but mature and highly fragmented; one industry estimate put 2025 market growth at only ~3.5% while the number of operating hot pot restaurants fell materially, reflecting consolidation pressure and a 'rational competition' phase that management says the industry entered in 2026 after a period of price-driven adjustment.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high - casual/mid-tier dining is discretionary spending sensitive to Chinese consumer confidence, employment conditions and the broader economic/property-sector slowdown.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct exposure given limited debt reliance; indirect sensitivity via consumer discretionary spending and corporate borrowing costs for expansion capex.
key_input_costs: Condiments/seasonings (partly sourced from related party Yihai International)
Commercial rent (though company owns/controls much of its real estate footprint via leases)

recent_developments.event: H1 2026 results: revenue up 7.9% YoY to RMB22,336.9 million; core operating profit up 4.4% to RMB2,513.5 million; profit up only 0.5% to RMB1,764.0 million; delivery revenue surged 121.2% to RMB2,051.4 million (9.2% of revenue, up from 4.5%); core Haidilao dine-in revenue fell 4.0% due to fewer self-operated restaurants; interim dividend of HKD0.377/share declared.

Company designated 2026 as the 'inaugural year' for building centralized 'middle office' management capability, shifting growth drivers from single-restaurant-manager-driven execution to headquarters-platform-driven operations; board/management changes included new executive director appointments in January 2026.

'Pomegranate Plan' sub-brand strategy shifted from broad exploration to focused replication: food-stall hot pot and sushi formats identified as having reached scalable, proven models and prioritized for resource allocation; other-restaurant revenue grew 113.1% to RMB1,271.4 million (5.7% of revenue).

FY2025 results: revenue grew only 1.1% to RMB43,225.4 million; core operating profit fell 13.3% to RMB5,403.2 million; profit fell 14.0% to RMB4,041.9 million, driven by declining table turnover (4.1x to 3.9x/day) and costs of innovation/scenario adjustments; 85 self-operated restaurants proactively closed/relocated; final dividend of HKD0.384/share proposed.

Same-store sales for self-operated Haidilao restaurants fell ~6.7% in FY2025 versus FY2024, with guest visits down 7.5% to 383.9 million, continuing a multi-year decline in core dine-in traffic amid intensified competition and shifting consumer preferences toward value and new dining formats.

Delivery business (including 'single-serving high-quality fast food'/rice-bowl products) became a key strategic focus, with over 1,200 delivery network points established nationwide and deep cooperation with all major Chinese delivery platforms.

items.target: Pace of new openings expected to increase versus 2026
items.notes: Management plans to accelerate new-store openings in quality shopping malls in higher-tier cities and lower-tier mass markets, leveraging middle-office-developed restaurant models, after a year of organizational consolidation in 2026.

items.target: Food-stall hot pot and sushi formats to scale from H2 2026, becoming a significant revenue growth source in 2027
items.vs_prior: raised (shift from broad exploration to focused, prioritized replication)
items.notes: No specific restaurant-count or revenue target disclosed; qualitative commitment to prioritize talent and site-selection resources toward these two formats.

items.target: More prudent/cautious approach to franchise expansion going forward
items.vs_prior: lowered (more cautious than prior rapid franchise rollout)
items.notes: Management explicitly flagged a more prudent approach to franchising 'on the basis of thorough review,' suggesting past franchise expansion pace will not continue unchecked.

items.target: Strategically pursue acquisitions of high-quality catering assets
items.notes: No specific deal size or target disclosed; qualitative strategic intent reiterated in both FY2025 annual report and H1 2026 interim report.

guidance.management_commentary: Chairman Zhang Yong and management describe 2026 as the 'inaugural year' for building middle-office management capability, shifting the Group's growth engine from restaurant-manager-driven execution to a centralized headquarters platform. Management explicitly frames 2027 as a year of parallel 'rejuvenation of existing operations and incremental expansion,' citing plans to upgrade/relocate aging restaurants, accelerate store openings versus 2026, prioritize the food-stall-hot-pot and sushi sub-brands for scaled replication, continue expanding delivery as a core growth pillar, and adopt a more prudent/disciplined approach to the franchise business while still citing an openness to M&A of high-quality catering assets.

bull_case: Delivery business is scaling extremely rapidly (+121% H1 2026) and could become a durable, higher-margin growth pillar as it diversifies beyond the hot pot dine-in occasion

Multi-brand 'Pomegranate Plan' incubation platform is beginning to show proof points (food-stall hot pot, sushi) that could replicate Haidilao's operational playbook across new formats and reaccelerate growth from 2027
Strong brand recognition and loyalty base (244M+ members) provide a platform for monetization even as same-store metrics normalize from pandemic-era highs
Management is taking credible, disciplined restructuring action (2026 'middle office' build-out, more prudent franchise approach, selective store closures) rather than ignoring the slowdown

Valuation appears to price in much of the bad news; consensus analyst targets (~HK$15-18) imply meaningful upside versus a depressed share price, and the company continues to pay a substantial dividend despite earnings pressure
bear_case: Core Haidilao dine-in brand, still ~80%+ of revenue, is in a multi-year structural decline in table turnover and same-store sales with no clear sign of stabilization as of FY2025/H1 2026
China's broader consumer discretionary spending slowdown and intensified value-oriented/delivery-platform price competition are secular headwinds, not one-off events

Margin erosion (core operating profit -13.3% in FY2025 despite +1.1% revenue) shows costs rising faster than Haidilao's ability to pass them through, and delivery/sub-brand growth carries lower margins and higher platform/marketing costs

Execution risk is high: the company is simultaneously restructuring its organization, scaling delivery, incubating 20+ sub-brands, and adjusting its franchise strategy, any of which could misfire as the 2022 'Woodpecker' closure debacle demonstrated
Highly fragmented, low-switching-cost industry limits Haidilao's ability to sustainably defend premium pricing, making its brand-based moat more fragile than scale alone would suggest
